articles.headline: White House Swaps Canadian Tariffs Like Items in a Fantasy Football Trade, Four Days Before Election
articles.dek: Trump removes some 50% duties on Canadian goods and adds valves, carpets and waste products, as Sen. Susan Collins claims credit for the exemptions in a tight Maine race.
articles.catch_up: Trump imposed 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods over the summer using Section 338, a 96-year-old trade law, as part of an escalating trade war. Maine, which imports more from Canada than from any other country, has felt the strain, and the tariffs are a top issue in its Senate race.
articles.why_it_matters: The net tariff burden on Canadian goods is not obviously shrinking, so businesses that import the newly covered products face higher costs even as others get relief. Consumers in border states and everywhere else should expect the tariff list to keep shifting.
body: The White House said Friday it would drop tariffs on some Canadian goods and replace them with tariffs on other Canadian goods, according to CNBC. President Donald Trump signed a proclamation removing certain products from the list he hit with 50% duties this summer. A fact sheet says the list will instead include "certain valves, carpets, waste products, and others." The administration describes this as an effort to refine the scope of the tariffs. A tariff list that is refined and not reduced is a bit like a diet in which you give up bread and take up pasta.

The sequence of events is the interesting part. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, announced that she had secured exemptions on nine categories of products she called crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, a claim The Wall Street Journal reported first. Her press release did not mention that new tariffs were coming. The White House announced the additions less than an hour later. Translation: the senator announced the good news, and the administration supplied the rest of it.

The exempted items, according to Collins, include corrugated paper, plastic boxes and packing bags, refrigeration equipment, multiple forms of machinery, and seaweed and algae products. Her spokeswoman, Phoebe Keller, told CNBC that Collins "requested exemptions for products that are important to Maine and will continue to do so." Asked what Collins had agreed to in her conversations with the administration, that is the answer CNBC received. The fact sheet does not mention Maine.

The timing carries its own message. The changes take effect Oct. 30, four days before the Nov. 3 election, and voters in Maine have already started casting ballots. Collins is fighting for reelection against Democrat Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger, and the tariffs are unpopular in the state. Jackson said Collins enabled the policy and now wants credit for "bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."

This is a rerun. At the Oct. 6 debate, Collins took credit for removing items such as road salt from the tariff list. Jackson replied, "What about everything else? We can't eat road salt." It is a fair point about a product that is useful mainly in winter and not at all for dinner.

The White House has a different framing. Spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC the proclamation responds to Canada's "continued discrimination" and retaliation against U.S. commerce, with the goal of restoring reciprocity. Translation: reciprocity means each side's tariffs are supposed to be matched by the other's, and the arrangement is that the matching never ends. Collins, for her part, said she would keep seeking relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada.

For markets, the swap is a footnote. SPY closed at 759.97 on Oct. 23 and the VIX stood at 19.03 on Oct. 22, which suggests investors have decided that tariff reshuffling is the weather. Inflation was 3.74% year over year as of September, and tariffs on inputs such as valves and packaging tend to show up eventually in the prices of things that contain them. Watch what happens after Nov. 3, when the political value of an exemption presumably drops and the next proclamation arrives.
articles.wire_headline: Trump dropping some Canada tariffs but 'replacing' them with other products

articles.headline: Trump Order Targets Mortgage Insurance, Hopes 7.32% Rate Will Look Smaller From Far Away
articles.dek: An executive order signed less than two weeks before the midterms would cancel mortgage insurance automatically on some future loans and make cheaper refinancing permanent.
articles.catch_up: President Trump signed an order titled "Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People" as rising rates and inflation squeeze buyers. It follows earlier orders, including one restricting Wall Street firms from buying single-family homes.
articles.why_it_matters: The changes could trim a few hundred dollars from some borrowers' costs, but the biggest drivers of housing affordability, home prices and mortgage rates, are untouched. Analysts quoted by CNBC say the full effect is hard to judge without more details.
body: President Trump has signed an executive order directing federal agencies to cancel mortgage insurance "proactively" on eligible future loans and to make a cheaper refinancing program permanent, CNBC reported. The order arrives less than two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, at a time when housing costs rank high among voter concerns. Timing, as ever, is a matter of coincidence.

Start with the insurance. Translation: private mortgage insurance, or PMI, is a fee borrowers pay to protect the lender, not themselves, when they put down less than 20% of a home's price. Currently, borrowers can generally ask to drop it once their balance falls to 80% of the original value, and servicers may remove it automatically at 78%. The order tells the Federal Housing Finance Agency to build a pilot program that cancels it without being asked once equity hits a certain threshold. It would apply only to mortgages originated after the pilot launches, so anyone currently paying is invited to admire it from the sidewalk.

The stakes depend on how much PMI costs. Fannie Mae puts it at 0.2% to 2% of the loan annually, depending on down payment, credit score and other factors. Freddie Mac's calculator, per CNBC, shows about $351 a month on a $600,000 home with 10% down and a 7.3% 30-year mortgage. FHFA director Bill Pulte said on X that "millions of Americans will save thousands and thousands of dollars." Keith Gumbinger of mortgage site HSH said it is hard to know the consumer impact without more details.

The industry's reaction was gracious. Seth Appleton of the mortgage insurers' trade group said it commends the focus on lowering costs and that the industry is "already delivering on that goal." Translation: the people who collect the fee are pleased that someone is looking into the fee.

The second piece concerns refinancing. The order makes permanent an FHFA pilot that waives the lender's title insurance policy, which protects the lender against disputes over who actually owns the house, and allows cheaper alternatives. Title-related charges are generally the largest part of closing costs, according to a 2025 Urban Institute report. Former FHFA director Sandra Thompson estimated in 2024 that borrowers could save $500 to $1,500 on loans under the pilot, which was limited to certain states and loans with a loan-to-value ratio below 80%.

Gumbinger was measured about the whole package. "I don't know that it's necessarily a game-changer," he said, noting that housing costs are dictated by home prices and mortgage rates. "Every little bit certainly helps," he added.

The rates are the larger problem. Freddie Mac put the 30-year fixed rate at 7.32% as of Oct. 23, and refinance demand was down 59% in mid-October from a year earlier. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, was 4.96% on Oct. 22, and CPI inflation was 3.74% in September. The Federal Reserve's latest survey found the monthly payment on a median-priced home took about 33% of median family income in 2025, up from 26% in 2022.

So the order shaves the edges of a cost that is mostly set elsewhere. Watch for the FHFA's pilot details, including the equity threshold and the start date, since those will show whether this is a savings plan or a press release with a closing date.
articles.wire_headline: Trump's executive order targets mortgage insurance, refinance costs. What it means for borrowers
